utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Judge Baird cannot be with us during the first session, due to his official engagement in another Chamber. I believe he will join us from the second session. So we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis during this first session. Ms. Sutherland, I was informed that you have something to raise before we begin today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. On Friday, Mr. Karadzic, during cross-examination, took the witness -- or put a proposition of another witness to Dr. Mandilovic, and I have looked through that particular witness's prior testimonies and a number of documents and wasn't able to find the proposition that Mr. Karadzic was putting to this witness. I would ask, in future, to be given a page number of the source of the assertion being put so that we can quickly check that. I didn't have the transcript of that other witness with me in the courtroom on Friday, and checked it subsequently. And as I said, if we could have a page reference number, that would be very helpful. And as I said, I also was not able to find that assertion or that proposition that was put to the witness in any of the witness's testimony that I was able to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. I believe Mr. Karadzic received that notice already, so I would like him to bear that in mind in the future cross-examination. Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am sorry. I just need to have a look at this and see what this relates to. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope that you understand my need to spell things out as precisely as possible and to establish what is a rumour and what is uncontested knowledge. Let me ask you, by the way: Did you talk to anyone about this over the weekend?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Telephone with the old country?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you have a scholarship from the military, or did you get a job with the military after you graduated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive a scholarship during my schooling from the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the first page of your statement, you said -- that is, your statement dated the 11th of January (as interpreted), 2000, that the JNA was a professional military organisation that was well organised, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that that the soldiers were conscripts rather than professionals?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers were recruited, they were conscripts, but the officers were professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 2 of that statement, you said that it was difficult to make a decision, and that, in fact, your departure from the unit was desertion. Do you continue to believe that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not my position. This was an informal conversation that was later used in my statement. That was stated hypothetically. I have been saying all the time that it was the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I were to tell you that the Yugoslav People's Army changed its composition in the following way: Officers who were Slovenes and Croats, and later on the others, simply left it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left it because the states of Slovenia, Croatia, Macedonia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, seceded from Yugoslavia and created their own armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that many of these officers left the army before these countries attained independence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible, but I do not have any knowledge to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of that statement, you say: "Hypothetically speaking, it would be possible that this may have been execution on the spot. However, I must add that I am not aware of any specific examples, so this was my opinion, and it is based on my experience from the JNA."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we're talking about the JNA. We talked about the establishment of the Yugoslav People's Army, not the former Yugoslav Army, rather, the Yugoslav People's Army, when Yugoslavia was a comprehensive state. We were talking about the Rules of Service. We were speaking hypothetically about the forms of murder. We were talking about high treason, and we said that capital punishment did exist for that. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about regular situations, or are you talking about emergencies, or are you talking about court-martials, as they were called?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discussion had to do with a regular situation in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Dr. Mandilovic: When you referred to the former Yugoslav Army, you referred to the VJ, and Yugoslav People's Army, to JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA. As the state disintegrated and as the republics acquired independence, it became the former JNA, the former Yugoslav People's Republic, practically from 1991 onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I don't know if Mr. Karadzic said "11th of January, 2000," but the statement is actually dated the 11th of February, 2000. That's at page 3, line 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have said "February." Thank you all the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what was it that you meant? From 1991, when were the republics actually recognised?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were recognised when they were recognised by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that's January 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that you asked me about Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Slovenia and Croatia too.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when they were recognised, but I know for sure that it was 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have to go back to this question of patriotic forces. The hospital was surrounded by patriotic forces, and an agreement was reached that equipment would be left behind. Let us see how much you know about this. What is it that you call patriotic forces, and what were the forces that exist in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Patriotic forces are the Territorial Defence, the regular police force, and the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Muslim part of Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the part of Sarajevo that was later under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Serbs from Grbavica, Vraca, Lukavica and so on, they weren't patriots; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they were. I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, you said his statement was taken on February 11th, 2010?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I said "11th of February, 2000." It was a prior statement of the witness that Mr. Karadzic was putting to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not the amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was confused about that. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic. Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, did you know that in addition to the Territorial Defence -- or, rather, do you agree that the Territorial Defence, according to federal law, was subordinated to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to federal law, yes. But don't forget that Bosnia-Herzegovina was proclaimed an independent state at the time that we are discussing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, none of us will ever forget that. Did you know when the Patriotic League was formed, and the Green Berets? Do you know that the decision was reached on the 31st of March, 1991, and that in April 1991 the Patriotic League was established, which, up until January/February 1992, grew to a force of, say, 120.000 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of these figures, Mr. Karadzic. I was not a member of the Patriotic League, I was not a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wasn't, either, but I know. I know that it was a force to reckon with, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if you wish to give evidence, you can do so. But at this time, just put your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandilovic, is this a convincing answer? You say, No, I don't know, I wasn't a member. Is it only members that know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me about 1991. 1991 was not a war year, and I was not really involved in any of that. I just did my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 3 - I think it's page 3 or 4 of your statement -- it's page 4 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that the State Hospital was not a military target, there weren't any military positions, there weren't any personnel -- military personnel within the hospital compound: "We were simply there to treat people. In spite of that, the hospital was intentionally targeted by mortar fire." First of all, tell me, was there a detachment or a battalion belonging to the Medical Corps there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the hospital after the 10th of May, 1992? It is not very clear, what this pertains to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandilovic, in your view, when was it that the Serbs intentionally shelled the Military Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shelling of the former Military Hospital started after the 10th of May, 1992, when the personnel of the former JNA started withdrawing from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the question. It is too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. The interpreters were quicker to note the problem with the quick -- the sequence of questions and answers, some of which are occurring while the interpretation is still taking place of the previous responses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was your point. Thank you, Mr. Tieger. As you can note from this transcript, the interpreters couldn't follow your question and answer because you overlapped and you spoke too fast. So if both of you slow down and put a pause between the question and answers. So could you repeat the previous question and answer, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mandilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to all participants in these proceedings, the interpreters in particular. But all of this rushes you to the fact that I haven't got enough time for this re-examination or cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, did you say that after the 10th of May, there was no medical battalion in the Military Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Military Hospital, which is now the State Hospital, there never was any military battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2111, could I have that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, could I ask you to read these 19 points?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Command -- the Command of the Corps, Military Unit," such and such a number. Do I need to read all of this out? This is a list of the temporary locations of the units of the 1st Corps, and then they are listed here: The Mountain Brigade, the 2nd Mountain Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. The first paragraph, can we read that: "On the basis of a need that was expressed and frequent requests coming from the unit, we hereby send you a review of the temporary locations of the units from the composition of the 1st Corps. "The Command Corps," number 1. "2. 1st Mountain Brigade, Sarajevo. "The 2nd Mountain Brigade --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Dr. Mandilovic. Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. Could the document be scrolled up so that we could see the date in the top of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, could you read this slower?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes: "The 1st Motorised Brigade, Danijela Ozme, Sarajevo; the 2nd Motorised Brigade, Dzemala Bijedica, Sarajevo; 5th Motorised Brigade, Dobrinja; 9th Motorised Brigade, Trampina, Sarajevo. 101st --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the witness needs to read out all the document. What is your point, Mr. Karadzic? You said point 19. What was your question? We can read it later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no translation, and I wanted this to be heard in the courtroom, what forces were involved here in April 1993. This is the organic composition of the 1st Corps, and nothing seems to be known about that here. Later on, they grew to the level of three divisions, out of which the 12th Division remained in Sarajevo. In many proceedings and trials here, Sarajevo was considered a harmless, helpless --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you read number 17?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we can see the substance of the document, as to the amount of brigades that there are, and you can deal with it in your evidence. So for other documents like this, simply put the question to the witness, and you can be assured that the meaning will be clear to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, could you read item 17?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Medical Battalion, Military Post 5751, Military Hospital (GA), Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. You lived in Sarajevo for a long time, just like me. Do you know where these streets are?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Danijela Ozme is right in the very center, right opposite the Presidency building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Vase Miskina is in the very center, it continues along Tito Street?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Trampina is close to the grand park in the center of town as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Nemanjina is also in the center of town, but it's a bit towards the slopes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again, Danijel a Ozme, the Military Hospital, and the Marsal Tito Barracks. All of this except for Dobrinja is in the center of town; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that Asim Dzambasovic signed this document, Dzambasovic, who is chief of staff of the 1st Corps, would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I accept it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I have an observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Medical Battalion was never part of the Military Hospital. We have to be very clear about this. The former Military Hospital, that is, the State Hospital, never had a military component to it, and I'm very positive and strenuous about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it says this is part of the corps, not part of the hospital. Was it deployed within the infrastructure of the Military Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not way. It was outside the Military Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Within the compound of the Military Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the compound of the Military Hospital, I agree, but far from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you said it was 300 metres to the River Miljacka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you forget that it spreads in the east-west -- along the east-west line. It is very narrow along the north-south line, but it's a very broad area along the east-west line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D496, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On this page, you said that despite that, the hospital was deliberately targeted by mortars. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply, the rest of 1992 and all of 1993, the city of Sarajevo was constantly shelled with artillery of various calibres indiscriminately in the immediate area of the Military Hospital. The shelling went on for 10, 12 hours non-stop, and we could clearly hear the detonations of the incoming projectiles and their falling very close to us. You must know that a shell of any artillery piece falls within the narrow core of the city, on concrete or on asphalt, and you cannot mistake that sound for anything else. And the projectile, itself, disintegrates into a huge number of shrapnel. There is no dilemma about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which outgoing fire did you mention? Which outgoing fire did you hear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Dr. Mandilovic. Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic said, page 13, line 1: "On this page, you said that despite that the hospital was deliberately targeted by mortars." Which page is Mr. Karadzic referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about page 4 of this statement, dated the 11th of February, 2000, and I do not mind at all if the doctor needs some breathing space to give an answer to this question. But, please, it is his statement, page 4 of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that wasn't my reason for standing up. The document -- the reference before had been to the amalgamated witness statement. Now he's going back to the February 2000 statement. So that was why I raised, because I couldn't see it on that page of that amalgamated witness statement or on the page of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Mandilovic, if you remember the question, yes, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I did not hear any outgoing fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, a moment ago you said that you heard outgoing and incoming fire?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Your question was whether I heard mortar fire or other kinds of artillery fire that was coming from the positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and going towards the forces of the Bosnian Serbs. That's what you meant, and I did not hear any such fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us try to refresh your memory now. I read this out to you, and I said, In spite of that, the hospital was intentionally targeted by mortar fire. I assumed that after the 10th of May, you are ascribing that to the Serbs, and my question to you was: How come you knew? And you said that you had heard outgoing fire and incoming fire, and you described what was falling around you, and so on. There was outgoing fire, and I'm going to show you what kind of outgoing fire that was. But I would be interested in hearing what it was that you heard.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two days ago, when I discussed this problem with you, I said that the positions of the Bosnian Serbs were very nearby, close to the centre of Sarajevo, that is, and, specifically, close to our hospital; also, that artillery positions were relatively nearby. So when I say "outgoing fire," I'm talking about the initial firing of shells or projectiles. And after a while, we would hear them fall in a particular part of town, and that created a great deal of noise. That's what I said, and that's what I'm repeating again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that you heard outgoing and incoming fire, and that both were Serbian fires, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. "Outgoing" is not a good term. That is initial fire created by detonation due to a projectile that was fired from an artillery piece. However, since there wasn't a classical front-line in Sarajevo, the distances were very short. So down there in town, in hospital, we heard the moment when artillery pieces fired from the hills and when these projectiles hit the city. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What hill are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire southern part of the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the slopes of Trebevic? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a rule, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far is the Jewish cemetery, as the crow flies, from the Military Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I've said this on a number of occasions. Six hundred or six hundred and fifty metres as the crow flies, perhaps. It's difficult for me to estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What sort of heavy artillery pieces did the Serbs have at the Jewish cemetery?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't visit the Serbian positions, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll have to go back to that subject when we receive some documents that we are waiting for. But you said, sir, that stress contributed to the fact that a lot of errors were made. On the same page: "Human nature is such that errors are made, but when providing a diagnosis or curing patients in the course of an artillery shelling, more mistakes are made." And so on and so forth. Can you mention some of these mistakes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's the translation that you have just read out. It's not in the spirit of our language. That's why it seems a little clumsy when you read it out. In our own language, it's different. What I want to say is that there was a lot of stress of all those who -- for all those who worked in the hospital. They were under a lot of psychological pressure. That concerned them and their families as well. That is what is at stake. The problem is that in such an uncertain situation -- well, such an uncertain situation went on for several months, not just for a day or two, and this can exhaust someone psychologically. In addition, I have to point out that there was also a lack of energy, a lack of heating. This also contributed to stress. I said that the temperature in the hospital was equivalent to the outside temperature on numerous occasions. You know that the climate is a continental climate in Sarajevo, so you can imagine what the temperature was like in the operation room or in the hospital wards. When this goes on for a lengthy period of time, then it's quite natural that your psychological equilibrium isn't what it usually is. As a psychologist, you're well aware of the fact. Another factor is the lack of food; a significant lack of food, not an absolute lack of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that, Doctor. But I am interested in whether these mistakes that you have mentioned had certain medical consequences, and if so, of what kind?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice any significant mistakes that would have affected the health of the patients that were in our care.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could just return to the matter. I do remember that statement, and I think that part of the statement also relates to the significant influx of wounded. On such occasions, it's possible for certain mistakes to be committed, given the significant influx of wounded and the various types of wounds involved. Then mistakes are quite possible. However, we did our best to avoid committing mistakes, to reduce the mistakes made to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you provide this statement in English or in Bosnian, as they say, originally?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Bosnian language, but it was then translated into English and then back into our own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5, you said that you couldn't say that the hospital was deliberately targeted by snipers, but you said that the hospital was hit on numerous occasions by fire from light weapons. Doctor, could you tell us the following: Where were the closest Serbian positions from which it was possible to see clearly the Military Hospital without any buildings hindering one's sight?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The positions -- the Serbian positions from which you can see the hospital is the entire Trebevic area, especially the western slopes of Trebevic. The Jewish cemetery, Grbavica, and Vraca are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And tell me the following: Was it possible to fire on the Military Hospital from Grbavica, given the layout of the buildings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was absolutely possible. Certain parts of the hospital could be fired on, and especially the more elevated parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, Major - I address you as Major now - what is the range for rifle fire?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is at the end of the 20th century. The weapons were sophisticated. Snipers had a range of over 1.000 metres, without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying 12.7 or 7.92?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a military specialist, Dr. Karadzic, but you know what I mean. The range is quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a look at that once we have received the map. You mentioned the lack of water, and you said that the water supplies were sometimes interrupted, but: "Since water was essential for the hospital, we had to improvise so that we always had water available. When there was no water, we would bring it in by lorries to the hospital. They would be kept in special reservoirs. In spite of all the difficulties, we always managed to have available water." Could the water of Miljacka be used for the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we were in the hospital, and we had water in the hospital for the basic needs. Where water was brought in from, I don't know, but its quality was controlled, it was disinfected, it was sterilised. That's certain. Our management took good care of the water supply and the energy supply. I wasn't directly concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since you know Miljacka, you must know whether the water could be put to good use.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we didn't have any cases of poisoning as a result of the use of water, so where the water was actually brought in from, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But could anything have been brought in from Miljacka? You and I are familiar with Miljacka. Could the water from Miljacka have been used?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're thinking of the river that passes through the town of Sarajevo, I don't think that would have been possible. It would have really been necessary to sterilise the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree at the time, in the part of Sarajevo under Muslim control, there were about 300.000 individuals?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's the correct figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that 50.000 to 60.000 individuals, out of those 300.000, were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which part of Sarajevo? What do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Throughout Sarajevo, in the entire Sarajevo, there were 175.000 Serbs and 24.000 Yugoslavs -- there were at least 15.000 Yugoslavs, so there were 180.000 Serbs, 175.000 Serbs in all of Sarajevo, but in the part that remained under Muslim control, there were 50.000 to 60.000 Serbs at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the daily consumption of water per individual in such -- or, rather, in normal conditions, is between 600 and 800 litres, but in such conditions, 100 to 120 or 180 litres daily would be the daily consumption of water?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that information, Mr. Karadzic. But as a member of the State Hospital, but also as a civilian, I know that there was very little water and that it had to be used with care. I really don't know where you have that information from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We went to the same university, we graduated from the same university. For an individual to function normally, such an individual needs between 600 to 800 litres of water a day. But given the conditions in Sarajevo, it would be 100 to 120 litres per person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can't talk about normal conditions. You have to reduce that amount quite significantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, the water that did arrive, where did it arrive from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for confirmation, Dr. Mandilovic, could you give the number of the individuals that were in the part of the Sarajevo under the Muslim control? Did you say 3.000 or 300.000?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was actually Mr. Karadzic that said the figure of 300.000, and I think the witness said, That's about correct, or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So 300.000. Thank you. It was Dr. Karadzic who said that. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 300.000, if I have understood this correctly, and the witness said that perhaps 50.000 to 60.000 of them were Serbs. That's the information that international institutions have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, where did the water come from? Which sources were under the control of the Muslim government?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He's asked that question three times and it's been answered already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you, Doctor, reject the possibility that Muslim authorities sabotaged the possibility of repairing the water supply system and making water available?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that the forces of the federal part of Sarajevo were involved in any acts of sabotage. It wasn't in the interest of the population that lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it in the interest of certain criminals to sell water? And if water was readily available, then the price of water would fall because they wouldn't be able to sell it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit that I didn't notice anyone selling water. That's quite interesting. Food would be sold, but I never noticed water being sold.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that the price of food will also vary, and when there wasn't a sufficient amount of food, the prices would be very high?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, do you reject the possibility that the Muslim authorities asked Hungary to reduce the pressure of gas and then exerted pressure -- or, rather, said that the Serbs weren't providing any gas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that information. This was something that occurred at an international, inter-state level, so I really didn't have the opportunity of finding anything out about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I were to tell you that the authorities in Sarajevo were, to a large extent, responsible for the lack of water and gas, and we'll demonstrate this here, we have information pertaining to that subject, if I said that, what would you say? Would you be angry with the Serbs or with them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't believe them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No probative value for us, questions which would require speculation on the part of the witness, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you'll see that it does have such value when we show certain documents. But the witness isn't aware of many things. I don't object to that, but I object to the fact that he says that Serbs did certain things, whereas he has no knowledge about the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, Doctor, did you say that there was a lack of medical supplies, of medicine, of anaesthetics, of oxygen, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, and that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you heard about the death of 12 babies in Banja Luka because no one made it possible for oxygen to be delivered for the incubators?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard about that. But I don't understand why that happened in Banja Luka. Banja Luka wasn't surrounded, and you can't compare the situation in Banja Luka to the situation in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the objection is obvious by way of relevance, and it is astonishing that the accused continues to complain about the amount of time he has for cross-examination when he ventures into areas such as this and into the kinds of arguments that he's been advancing during the course of this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I quite agree with you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Karadzic, come to your question that is relevant to the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think I have good reason to test the credibility of the witness -- or, rather, to test whether the witness is well-informed. I don't mean to say that he is deliberately stating certain things that are detrimental, not only to me but to the Serb people as well, but I have the right to prove that the witness lacks certain knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just put your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this has not yet been entered into the e-court system, could we have this part here? Could it be placed on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, reading a map shouldn't present a problem.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the map. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you received the map, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If this is the same one that was in an e-mail at 2.13 p.m. this afternoon, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that different from the map which appears on page 8 of the Sarajevo binder, court binder?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think we have this. No, it's different, different. This is a map of the Muslim commander. [In English] Could you lift it a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I believe it is, Your Honour, it is different.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay, I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, can you find your way here, and can you tell us where the Military Hospital is and where the Jewish cemetery is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's try. [In English] May I? Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you should point to the actual map in order for us to follow. It's not in the e-court system. Just a second. Do you have another copy -- do you like the witness to mark the map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Maybe we have this in electronic form. Let's see. Maybe it is in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then proceed to mark it, if you are able to locate it. The question is whether you can recognise the place for Military Hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. Can you place "VB" or "GB "there, whatever you prefer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or "MH," whatever. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "SH" for "State Hospital." [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you find the Jewish cemetery now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you can use the red one. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't it a bit to the left, to the south? Can't you see the markings? No, no, that's the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've been through a variation of this before, so I think we need to be careful about who's marking the map. The witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the doctor will mark it only when he agrees with it. Dr. Mandilovic, did you follow me? So you agree with that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks] Roughly, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, do you agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I mean, I presume these locations are fixed objects within the city. They're not going to be in dispute, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm less concerned about the prospect of reaching agreement on where fixed locations are as I am about locations, the boundaries of which -- or the particular locations of which at the time of the examination may not be so clear to either the parties or the witness, in particular, and then having been -- having reluctantly agreed to place a location in a particular area, questions are posed on that basis as if it was a fixed and agreed area. So it's not that, in the abstract, that consensus can't be reached, but the use of a location as precise, when it was placed there by a witness who's only approximating and doing so on the basis of guidance by the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I don't see the difficulties, for instance, with a potentially mobile front-line of either party in the dispute. But when we talk about a hospital or a cemetery, in my experience, they don't move very far.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I agree, Your Honour, although if we are -- then we have to be cautious later, when markings are made in this fashion, that some effort is made to arrive at a consensus understanding of where that location might actually be and what the ambit of the area encompassed by that location may be, to the extent it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. If I may. If this map, which is on ELMO, is the same map as what was e-mailed by the Defence at 2.13 or whatever this afternoon, then it's in e-court, 65 ter number 11786. And I note the map is from March 1995 to 1996, May 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if I may follow up on His Honour Judge Morrison's question. I would also say in response, Your Honour, then it seems to me if the precise locations are really the point of such an exercise, and we could arrive at them in advance, save the Court a lot of time, and be confident that we actually had them identified, one has to wonder about the reason for continually engaging in this kind of a cartographic exercise in court when the witness is repeatedly evidencing reluctance to do so, discomfort with doing so, and uncertainty in doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, that's exactly why I raised the issue. I mean, Dr. Karadzic, presumably, when we're talking about fixed objects like hospitals, cemeteries, other notable buildings, this is a matter where an agreed -- all of those could be put on an agreed plan with the Prosecution, could they not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll let the accused respond. I had some additional information, but let me -- the Court put a question. I won't get in the way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we agree out of court on the weapons around the Military Hospital? Obviously, we cannot. We cannot agree on the distances, either, say, between the Jewish cemetery and the hospital. So let us identify this map. This is the working map of the chief, Rizvo Pleh signed it. Now, I would like the central zone to be zoomed in. Have a bit of faith in my lawyerly skills. I know exactly what I'm trying to say and what I'm trying to show, and we cannot settle that out of court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Tieger. Do you have any further point?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Only to note that the matters that Dr. Karadzic just raised are distinct from the precise locations that we were talking about. And I would also note that approximately 10 days ago, we provided, in response to a request by the Court, a map with such locations, and hoped that we would be able to arrive at some kind of resolution, so we're still awaiting a response from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on. Let's zoom in this e-court -- map in the e-court so that we can identify the relevant portions. No, if you can zoom in in the actual size, 100 per cent, we can find it. Zoom further. Again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A bit to the east. And now a bit further down. No, the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Going up. Yes. Further, further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, could we ask you to mark the Military Hospital and the Jewish cemetery?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, we have a bit of a clearer copy, and it's a blow-up of one part of this big map that I've just taken you to, and it's 65 ter number 07048J.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's not the very same map, the work map of the chief of staff, it's of no use to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It is the same map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we try it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you zoom out a bit, and could we see the eastern part. Now we just see a part, so we need to zoom out a bit. If you can't do better than that, then we can't see the Military Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the Jewish cemetery, Doctor, and do you see that the Muslims are on one side and that the Serbs are on the other side of that cemetery? Maybe we'd better go back to the previous map, because we cannot see the Military Hospital, which is what we want to see, on this map.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. You cannot see the State Hospital here. If you could lower it down a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or we can zoom out once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately, the map finishes here where it was actually on the screen, so it doesn't go high enough for the State/Military Hospital on this inset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then why don't we carry on with the actual map, which is on the ELMO. Yes, let's proceed with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then we can scan that map and up-load in the e-court. We proceed with the actual map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, while we're waiting, can I ask you whether you know where Avde Jabucice Street?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Livade is in that street?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Livade is in that street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's that area where there are no buildings, where nothing had been built yet.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Crni Vrh is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this now. There's the Jewish cemetery, there's the Military Hospital. What is this above the Military Hospital at Crni Vrh? Actually, is that Crni Vrh above the Military Hospital, where we see this marking here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot see any marking or figure. I don't know what you're saying, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're a major. Isn't this a marking for a howitzer or a cannon?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I really see no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this thing that looks like a syringe? Could you please put a circle around Crni Vrh, that area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's that neighbourhood, Doctor, but I don't want to correct you. Do you see where it says "Gorica" up here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but Crni Vrh and Gorica is practically one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that built-up area. I'm talking about the area about two centimetres away. Doesn't it say "Gorica" there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you put a circle around Crni Vrh, and can you tell me what that marking is at Crni Vrh?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a marking denoting an artillery piece. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please put a circle around that. Is that a Serbian gun or cannon, Major?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not a Serbian cannon, but I have no idea what cannon you're talking about. It is certainly not a Serbian cannon, because that part of town was not under the control of the Bosnian Serbs. Now, where this map came from and who made this map, I really have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll deal with that later. Do you see this, the "105th Mountain Brigade"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is that marking there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The "105th Mountain Brigade," and that's a tank there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please put a circle around that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you place the letter T there or simply write "Tank"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that a Serb tank, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea whether there is a tank there. I have never seen it there. This is just what you're suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But what does this military mark denote?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the military mark that we are talking about, but I cannot confirm for you something that I had never seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see another mark, semicircular, to the north-west of this one that we talked about just now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. [Indicating]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a symbol for mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you circle that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And could you mark "MB" by that place, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, could we go back to Gorica. Would you agree that immediately below this cannon, there are several streets that are called Avde Jabucice, they are sort of meandering streets of a kind?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a very steep and narrow street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark that with the letters "AJ"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's between the Military Hospital and Gorica; isn't that right? And could you mark the cannon position with a T or an H? It's obviously a howitzer.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what it is; I don't. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But there's no doubt that that is a symbol for a cannon, for an artillery piece?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know who put it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please date this and sign it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have the whole map again so that we can see what the distance is between the Military Hospital and the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, we have the scale of the map down below. I would say that this is about a thousand metres, one kilometre. You have the scale in the lower part of the map, and you can check the scale, you can check the distance.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that distance is incorrect. It's a far shorter distance, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look. Can you open up the map and have a look at the scale?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't need the scale, Mr. Karadzic. I can see the Jewish cemetery every day, and I can see details there. I can't see any details from a distance of one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we scroll down and see whether you agree that this is Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where Debelo Brdo is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Please date it, sign it. We will then scan it and file it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] I've never seen this map before, though, because this map is practically a map that I've just been shown, so I can't confirm that it's an authentic -- an adequate map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that you are responsible for the map. But you're a major, and the map demonstrates the artillery positions, where the artillery positions are above the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I sign the map, it means that I accept the map and I accept the fact that the ABiH was deployed in this manner, and this is not my opinion; therefore, I cannot sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see whose map it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it is not for the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regardless of whose map it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We understood your position, Dr. Mandilovic, rest assured. So did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't signed it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You recognised the place for the Military Hospital, and also you confirmed the location of the Jewish cemetery, and you just recognised the marking or the markings which would mean the artillery, or separate from the issue of whether that artillery actually existed at the time. So with that caveat, we'll admit that document. So if you are happy with that, so you can sign it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. With those reservations, yes, I will sign the map, because I'm not saying that those artillery positions were really there at the time. But as far as the positions of the hospital are concerned, the Jewish cemetery position, and the position of the street, well, naturally, there's no doubt about those positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We understood that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D497.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, did you have something to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was simply going to make the point that Mr. Karadzic is again making comments when he shouldn't be, and, secondly, that as the witness just said, he was directed to those markings by Mr. Karadzic and then circled them himself, but he is only sure about the Military Hospital, the Jewish cemetery, and the other street that he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And in some cases, he understood what those markings meant, so that's the furthest frame of the witness's evidence. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, I'd make one further point. I understand that's -- that the date of the map was 1995. I would think that when such documents are being presented to a witness, it would be helpful to indicate to the witness the relevant date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll bear that in mind in analysing the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, can you have a look to the south of Jewish cemetery. You can see that it says "Debelo Brdo" there. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't see that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's in the e-court system, not on the ELMO. It's in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It looks like it's the ELMO -- no, it isn't. It's in the e-court system. Could you assist us, perhaps? Could you assist Dr. Mandilovic and provide him with the map or make it possible for him to see the map that we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have the same map on the screen, the one that we were looking at just a minute ago? We have it in e-court system. It could be marked and signed. I'm talking about the previous map. All we have to do is switch the e-court system on. Have you got that now, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. I can see the Jewish cemetery, but I can't see the Military Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, I'm referring to Debelo Brdo, not the Military Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you circle that? It says "Debelo Brdo" there. Can you just circle it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we have the date and your initials, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Actually, I don't see the point, Mr. Karadzic. You are simply wasting your time. We can read "Debelo Brdo" in this map. Why do we need the witness to mark this "Debelo Brdo" at all?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Debelo Brdo was taken over by the Muslim Army, and the Muslim artillery was positioned there. It faces the Military Hospital. You can see the Military Hospital better than from the Jewish cemetery. There are no buildings that hinder one's sight. We'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can adduce evidence from another witness who can testify to that effect, but asking this witness, Dr. Mandilovic, to mark the location of Debelo Brdo in this map, which you can do easily without the assistance of this witness, is simply a waste of your time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The doctor said that what came from the hill, from Trebevic, were, in fact, Serbian shells. This is something we have to clarify. Were Serbian shells fired from there or not? This entire slope was in the control -- under the control of the Muslims. The doctor isn't aware of the fact. I don't object to that, but he can't claim that they are Serbian shells. That's what I object to. Will it be admitted or not? I'll get to my question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll just add one more point to the point the Court was making, and that is: The first question that Mr. Karadzic asked about Debelo Brdo: "Can we scroll down and see whether you agree that this is Debelo Brdo?" And the answer was: "I don't know where Debelo Brdo is." So not only are we engaging in the unnecessary exercise of marking and circling an area on a map that says Debelo Brdo, which clearly anybody can do, but we're doing it with someone who has previously indicated that he can't be of assistance in that regard, and I don't think we should encourage this kind of practice by admitting this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the witness said that he didn't know where Debelo Brdo is. But, Dr. Karadzic, we can admit the unmarked one, but I don't see any point of admitting this marked version of this map. There's no point. So we can admit the unmarked version, and I take it there should be no objection from the Prosecution. So if you are minded to tender this unmarked version, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender it. I'm convinced that the Chamber has the opportunity to see the deployment of forces around Debelo Brdo and the Jewish cemetery, and it's the first time you have had such an opportunity. So I suggest that this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This clean version will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D498, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D2109 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, Doctor, do you know that the Supreme Command Staff wanted the Sarajevo Military Hospital to be transformed into a military hospital again -- or, rather, to a hospital for the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with the details. Perhaps such request was made, but it was never put into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at that document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am looking at it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see it says "The Military Hospital, Special Institute," and so on and so forth? Do you know that such attempts were made -- such requests were made by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps, but I'm not familiar with the details. And this was never put into effect. That's what's most important.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at the following page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before we move on, can you see the first page? Dr. Mandilovic, can you recognise what document is -- this is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've never seen this document before, but I can see what it's about. It's a request. I saw the signature a minute ago. It's a request from the chief of staff of the ABiH, and it says that for the needs of the Armed Forces of the ABiH a medical centre should be established and organised, and in their opinion the former military hospital was the most appropriate hospital for providing the wounded and officers with care; because of its experience. I can see a stamp, I can see a signature here, so that's probably an authentic document, but, again, I'll repeat what I have already said: This was never put into effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Doctor, what this means, "The French Hospital," because -- was it called the French Hospital at one point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the 10th of May, after it had been taken over, after the former Military Hospital had been taken over by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 10 days after that event, as I have already said, a new name was given to it. "The State Hospital" is what it was called, and this was certified as the correct name. But at one point in time, I think it's when President Mitterrand visited Sarajevo - I remember this very clearly, he visited the hospital - at that point in time there was an idea according to which the civilian hospital could be under the auspices of the French -- or, rather, the name "The French Hospital" could be used, but that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at the last page so that we can see the commander, Sefer Halilovic, actually sent this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that correct, that's "Sefer Halilovic" there, and we have the stamp of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said a minute ago that it's an authentic document. I've never seen it before. I wasn't in such a position to have access to such a document, but there were rumours according to which such a transformation might occur. But as I have already said, this was never put into effect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D499, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, would you agree there were conflicts in 1992 between the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and between the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO, and that there were wounded and dead?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, as far as I can remember - a lot of time has passed since then - I think that at that time there were no clashes between the ABiH and the HVO. Naturally, we're speaking about the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were there any armed conflicts between them at a later date?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think there were certain disagreements and misunderstandings later on. I think there were certain low-level conflicts as well, but this was somewhat later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D2110, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While waiting for the document: Doctor, how were these victims described, the victims of the internal conflicts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. We were surrounded for a long time in Sarajevo. We had no contact with those who were wounded or who were ill outside the boundaries of the town of Sarajevo, so I can't really answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you read out what you can see here, what has been circled? Can we have a look at the bottom part of the document. Could you please read it out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We also have information according to which, in the evening hours on the 27th of December [Realtime transcript read in error "September"], 1992, a conflict broke out between members of the so-called BiH TO and the HVO. There was a conflict in the area between the tobacco factory, the School of Economics, and the French Hospital, and it lasted for five hours." I've already provided my answer, and I stand by that answer. If there were any clashes, I'm not aware of them, but one should point out that the conflicts that did break out could have been conflicts between certain unofficial bodies, between certain military formations that were out of control, so I really couldn't go into the details and comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would these informal groups be? You mean military groups that are out of control. Which ones?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, in the first stages of the war in the town of Sarajevo, the conditions were very difficult, and naturally certain informal groups were established. That wasn't just a characteristic for the ABiH. That was a characteristic of all the armies that were involved in the war in the Balkans. So there were groups led by certain criminals. At certain points in time, they wanted to take advantage of the situation. But these were low-level conflicts, and they didn't have a significant influence on the situation in Sarajevo and on the relationships that prevailed in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll deal with it after the break. We need to rise right now. The first break will be for 35 minutes. We'll resume at 3.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just a matter for the transcript. On page 42, line 12, the witness's -- the witness was asked to read out the last paragraph on this document that's on the screen, and it says in the transcript "27th of September, 1992." I don't know if that's what the witness actually said or whether he said "December," which is the correct date, 27th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the document reads "27th of December." Is it correct, Dr. Mandilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When I said that we would deal with the admission of this document after the recess, I was wondering about the relevance of this document. But you do not object to the admission of this document, separate from the issue of translation, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness hasn't been able to speak to anything in this document, and according to your guide-lines, then, it's my position that it shouldn't be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I was also wondering how it is related to the evidence of this witness which was given in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I've been waiting for the interpretation. Well, this is what this is about: The fighting between the HVO and the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was taking place in the vicinity of that hospital. Obviously, the wounded would be admitted to that hospital, and if there are fatalities, that would be the same thing. So that's the French Hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Instead of making submissions, you can put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I had put a question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, did your hospital bear the name of "French Hospital" for a while, and is it referred to as the place where there was fighting between the HVO and the Territorial Defence of the BH?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did bear the name of the French Hospital for a while, that's correct, but I did explain a few moments ago that in this triangle that you were talking about, the hospital, the economic school, and the factory of tobacco, there was no conflict. You know full well that the HVO is in the system of defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it was located at Stup, and that is very far away from the French Hospital or the State Hospital. Therefore, I cannot accept this document of Mr. Predrag Ceranic. I have read it, but I do not stand by what it says. This is just an approximate version, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, while the witness testified to the so-called low-level conflicts, but the witness didn't have any idea about this document, so we'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, let's just see this: Do you know where Trscanska Street is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it goes from Titova towards Silvije Kranjcevica, or, rather, the street where the Military Hospital is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bit further away from the Military Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far away?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A couple of hundred metres. Is it between the Military Hospital and the Unis skyscrapers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer is yes.
