utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Alpina is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you don't know where Alpina is in Trscanska Street?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that in Trscanska Street, in the Alpina building, there was the Command of the 2nd Battalion of the 243rd Light Croatian Brigade, of the HVO, that is, do you rule out that possibility or do you allow for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow for that possibility, but it wasn't a typical location for the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, Doctor, Stup is a Croatian neighbourhood, but Kralj Tvrtko, Marin Dvor [Realtime transcript read in error "Mali Zvornik"], is that a predominantly Croatian neighbourhood as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's predominant, but there certainly are Croats living there like in the other parts of Sarajevo for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Marin Dvor, not "Mali Zvornik," as the transcript says. Marin Dvor. I'm sorry I'm in such a rush, but the point is that I don't have enough time. Doctor, do you allow for the possibility or do you rule out the possibility that at Livade, in Avde Jabucice Street, mortars were taken out of garages, then they were used from time to time, and then they were taken back to garages, and that's what went on throughout the war, and that that was the outgoing fire that you could have heard?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of this, from you, here and now. I never saw that, personally, and I never heard anyone talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility or do you rule out the possibility that in front of the Military Hospital, there was a gun from time to time, a cannon, used to operate against Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely rule out that possibility. You know the configuration of the Military Hospital full well. You know that it's in the very centre of town. You know full well that it is practically inserted between two streets, and anyone who knows anything about artillery and artillery pieces would have to rule that possibility out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to bring those documents later. Tell me, Doctor, do you know that mortars also fired from the compound of the Kosevo Hospital and also there was a cannon nearby there as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us be very specific. I'm not accusing you of doing anything on purpose. However, when you say that some shells had come from Serb positions, do you have any proof of that or are you inferring that on the basis of the fact that there were Serb positions on the southern slopes, the slopes of Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already spoken about that. The entire area of the hospital and of Marin Dvor was shelled from Trebevic. And since Serb forces were at Trebevic, it was obvious that the fire came from there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to recommend the testimony of Mr. Mandilovic to the participants here, dated the 17th of January, 2007, in the case against General Milosevic. 558 [as interpreted] is the page number, the 17th of January, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you told us that you don't know where Debelo Brdo is, and also that Serb positions were at Trebevic, and that the shells that fell from Trebevic on the city were Serb shells. Let me read out to you now what happened on this page. I have to do this in English. The lawyer asked you the following -- it was Mr. Tapuskovic: [In English] "I just received the answer, and since the witness doesn't know, I wasn't assisting so much --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 558 is page 2 of his evidence-in-chief, so if I could be taken to the correct page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "588." I hope, at least, that I said "588."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can he carry on, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "I didn't insist on whether the Muslim forces were there. This is going to be proven in some other testimonies. I am only asking you whether Debelo Brdo -- the elevation of Debelo Brdo, and in the way he showed us, indicates that the Jewish cemetery was very close to the bottom of Debelo Brdo. Yes or no?" [Interpretation] And this is what you said: [In English] "Below Debelo Brdo, but I don't know who held Debelo Brdo." And so at that time, you didn't know where Debelo Brdo was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never knew where Debelo Brdo was. I know the term, but I don't know where it is. During the discussion and during the cross-examination, it was my understanding that Debelo Brdo was above the Jewish cemetery. And then I said, Well, yes, possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to draw page 604 to your attention, the 18th of January, 2007. I'm going to read it out to you now. Did you state your views on Colina Kapa during that trial as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know of Mala and Velika, Colina Kapa, but I don't know where they are. They are somewhere in the eastern part of Sarajevo, but I don't know where. Somewhere below Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what it says here. The question was on page 604: [In English] "Thank you very much. You spoke about this yesterday, and I don't want to dwell on that, but let me ask you: The two points, Colina Kapa and Debelo Brdo, they are the two dominant points and, of course, the hills of Trebevic?" [Interpretation] This was your answer: [In English] "What do you mean when you say 'the dominant points'? "Q. Well, these are two hills, too. One is almost a thousand metres high and the other is maybe 800. I can't remember the exact heights. Would those be the hills that dominated the hospital?" And you said: "Yes, yes." [Interpretation] Do you allow for the possibility or do you know, in fact, who was at those hills -- on those hills?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to make a certain correction; not in terms of what I said, but in terms of how it's been interpreted. Colina Kapa is pretty far away from the hospital, quite far away. It's at the periphery of town. These hills are not as high as you say. These are small hills, in relation to Trebevic, and -- and they do not have any great tactical importance, and they are of no strategic importance whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you do know what their strategic and tactical importance is; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, but one fact is for sure. Wherever the BH Army was, the army of the Bosnian Serbs was always above them. So the low hills that you refer to are absolutely unimportant, from a strategic point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that Colina Kapa is at a lower altitude, lower than 800 metres?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You can find that on a map. First of all, you have to look at the altitude of Sarajevo, and then the altitude of Colina Kapa. We should not confuse the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to show that, if we're given an opportunity, perhaps even during the course of your own testimony. Very well. What was the defence function of your hospital during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The State Hospital had the classical function of any health institution that is in a state of war. Namely, we took care of the wounded and the sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not take care of it at all, as if it were its own, and they did not feel that they had any right to do so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The State Hospital was a civilian structure. It had its own management, and, unfortunately, throughout the war it had to fend for itself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2108, please, could we have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the text below, just the first sentence that says: "I also ask you ..."? Actually, can you identify this? Is this a document of the Ministry of National Defence, the Staff of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who's it sent to, addressed to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The PTT Service of the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. They're asking for some numbers here; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please have a look at the sentence underneath the figures, the numbers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We also kindly request that you look into the possibility of assigning five new PTT numbers for the needs of the former Military Hospital."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this signed by Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, this seems to me like care about the Military Hospital, and also claiming the military as one's own, asking for additional telephone numbers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not any kind of particular care, Mr. Karadzic. This is mere necessity. After the destruction that came from you, or, rather, your forces, in terms of PTT facilities in the town of Sarajevo, there was chaos in the town of Sarajevo. It was extremely difficult to communicate. Since the town of Sarajevo was at war, everything is subjected to the military command, including PTT. It is only natural that the Military Hospital -- rather, the former Military Hospital, now the State Hospital, as a civilian structure, addresses the military command to ask for approval. You know that in war, there is only a military command and that it's only the military that has jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that there was military administration in the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, far be it from the truth. I'm just saying that certain functions were under the military. For example, the assigning of telephone numbers for normal communication in such an important health institution does not mean that this institution is under the control of the military. I've already said that, and I stand by that. You don't have a single relevant document stating that the State Hospital was under the military throughout the war. This is just normal assistance in a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, why didn't your director, your general manager, ask for this? Why was it the commander of the staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our manager must have asked, but he addressed the chief of staff to make sure that they get this PTT line through him. As I said, this was of vital importance, PTT, et cetera, and it has to be under the military in a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. So he asked the commander of the Main Staff to obtain this for him. He asked him -- he made this request, since it was sent to his superior; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. Mr. Sefer Halilovic was never our director's superior, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you something else. Do you know anything about Markale I, about the incident, the tragedy, however you want to call it? It was February 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 5th of February, 1994. There was a large-scale massacre that occurred on that occasion. I remember it. I wasn't on duty at the time, but according to the information I was provided with -- in the late afternoon, I arrived in the hospital. Much medical care had already been provided. It really was a large-scale massacre. There were many wounded, and many people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ask Ms. Sutherland not ask you about Markale I, but only about Markale II?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask anyone for anything. I haven't done so in the past, and I'm not doing so now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, we'll admit the previous document as MFI Exhibit D500.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your supplemental information sheet, the first item on the first page says the following: [In English] "People would be terrified and lapse into depression, and eventually could become indifferent and, apparently, fatalistic. This is a progression and indicative of psychological exhaustion. After a while, we seem to adapt to the fear."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have the date of the supplementary information sheet?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: This is supplemental, date 2nd of October 19 -- 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And at the top, it says the "22nd of November, 2001," supplemental information sheet. Doctor, what is this called, in scientific terms? How does one arrive at such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I have already said that. That's what I stated. I stand by what I stated there. According to my information, I have my knowledge from the sphere of psychology, psychiatry. Well, I said what I knew, and I didn't go into the details, but I do stand by what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that a precise scientific fact or is this your impression?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my impression. It's not an exact science. I wasn't involved in the science. There are people who were involved in that science. But this was my personal impression, as a person who, nevertheless, does have a certain amount of medical experience and knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the following page, you say: "I haven't noticed symptoms in those close around me ..." [In English] "... in people at large. Particularly, you see this in traffic, the impatience, nervousness, agitation. They break traffic rules and have alteration," probably, "[indiscernible] symptomatic of stress, PTSD effect." [Interpretation] Was a scientific study made which is the basis for what you claimed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, there were many scientific studies that were carried out in the war that continued from 1992 to 1995. Many such studies were made that, in particular, concerned the victims of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which studies are you referring to here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not basing my opinion on studies here. I was asked what my personal opinion was about the matter, so this statement isn't based on a scientific study of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next item says: [In English] " ... military doctors before. I did not know anything about how the VRS operated. They had come from JNA and had the same command staff, so it is logical that they worked in the way of the old JNA. I do not include paramilitaries in this. I never had contact with any of them." [Interpretation] Do you know where Muslim officers came from, ABiH officers, Sefer Halilovic, Nadalic [phoen], Hajrulahovic, and so on and so forth? Which army did they come from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officers, whose names you have mentioned, came from the JNA, that's what it says here, but there were officers in the ABiH who didn't have a military pedigree, who had come from other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you heard of Caco, Juka Prazina, Celo -- a certain Celo, and have you heard of their brigades and of the terror that they spread against the Serbs in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of the names that you have mentioned. They come from the town of Sarajevo, from that milieu. They weren't specific to the Sarajevo battle-field -- or, rather, there were paramilitary formations present amongst all the armies that were established. They had certain disagreements, they had certain problems. And during one period of time in the course of the war, the ABiH really strove to unite all those units and to place them under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with an army in the Balkans, or anywhere in the world, where criminals, such as Juka Prazina, became a general and a member of the supreme command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Juka Prazina was never a general in the ABiH. He moved over from the ABiH to the HVO for certain reasons that I can't comment on. I'm not familiar with all those situations. And there, he was promoted to the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you heard of Kazani, the place Kazani, which is where Serbs and Jews were killed, and does this remind you of the Second World War at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of Kazani only after the end of the war, after 1995. It was mentioned in the press, in the media, certain investigations were launched, but I know nothing else about that. As to the outcome of the investigation, I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How was this described to you? What did you hear about it after the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I knew was what I learned from the media, electronic media or the printed media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you learn about the event?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kazani was a place where certain Serbs were killed. That was the crux of the matter. That's a bit approximative. Definite conclusions were never reached with regard to the numbers concerned or the time-period, because a thorough investigation was never launched into that, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just wondering where the relevance of this [indiscernible] to the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I quite agree. I don't understand, Mr. Karadzic, how come you can complain about the shortage of time, asking these questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if this witness says the Serbs were targeting the hospital from Trebevic, they were doing that deliberately, and if he doesn't know who was on Trebevic, if he says it was terrible to live in Sarajevo at the time, we should find out who was responsible for this. If he says that the inhabitants of Sarajevo suffered, well, I know, but let's see why. This cannot be ascribed to the Serbs. Could we please see 1D2103. With all due respect for the witness, his statements have been made in a fairly cavalier manner. He's been expressing his impressions. He hasn't provided us with information about the conditions in Sarajevo for the Serbs, and these are the terrors that have to be described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is item -- this is from "Srna," 8th of May, 1992. It's a report from "Srna." Could we now see page 4 in this article, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As someone born in Novi Sad, I'm quite convinced that you can read the Cyrillic script without any problems. It says: "This is a dramatic appeal from the doctors who work in the Military Hospital in Sarajevo." It was sent on the 7th of May, 1992, to the Service for Informing the Crisis Staff. It says -- well, could you read out what it says here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Gentlemen, please prevent -- gentlemen, use all your forces to prevent the lies that are being spread with regard to this institution. There are no hostages here. No one has been isolated here. Only those who don't want to hand this institution over to the TO of the BH have remained here. I'm afraid that the authorities might be responsible for this house falling. We have some forces for our defence, but for five days now we haven't received any bread or milk. What have you done? We have been left here, and we are being targeted by mortars and snipers every day. You can't be heard. You are not doing anything. If you lose this house, you've lost half of Sarajevo. Please --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I think we have an English translation for this. No? Thank you. Please carry on, Dr. Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "You can't be heard. You are not doing anything. If this house is lost, you will have lost half of Sarajevo. Please announce that all soldiers in the military hospital are alive. Colonel Dusko Kovacevic is with us. Gentlemen, do something as soon as possible."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Colonel Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at the time you were absent there, do you know that they opened fire on the Military Hospital, snipers and mortars targeted the hospital, and they weren't provided with bread and milk for five days? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer the question. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you arrived there, did you ask about the situation when you were absent?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I arrived there, there was no one present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: None of those who complained; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, no one was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you notice the damage inflicted by the bullets or the mortars? Did you notice it on the 10th or the 12th, when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in the hospital, I didn't notice anything. I've already said that. I didn't notice any significant or extensive damage, not on the asphalt, or on the facade, on the walls, or on windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know -- did you notice minor damage?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. Eighteen years have passed since then. I can't remember. At the time, it wasn't important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Those people who were crying out for help think that that was important. Do you know who was shooting, until the 7th or the 10th of May, who was shooting at the Military Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you rule out the possibility that it was the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think you exhausted your topics -- I think you covered this topic at the beginning of your cross-examination. Move on to another topic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Pursuant to your guide-lines, Your Honour, I would -- it's our position that it shouldn't be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to be a bit cautious, Your Honour. Since we have engaged with discussions about the Defence with this, and we have had some discussions in court and Chambers about this, I'm not suggesting that every time a witness can't speak to the document or a document is presented to him to amplify some aspect of a cross-examination, it's not admissible. But in this case, in light of the fact that we have a time-period preceding the period about which the witness can use, and we have -- the document tendered is "Srna," which is the Serbian press agency, promulgated for particular reasons, I think we have a particular reason for caution here. So I don't want to suggest that we are re-introducing a more stringent form of admissibility, but I think the caution, as Ms. Sutherland expressed, with respect to these kinds of documents, is appropriate. I'm looking at Judge Lattanzi. She's -- I don't know if she has any questions about it, but I think "Srna" has a -- is a matter of a different kind of concern than normally official documents, the type we've been looking at coming from -- that are produced contemporaneous; for example, communications within particular bodies and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, "Srna" is a state news agency. It does not invent things. It doesn't provide comments. I don't rely on their comments. I rely on them conveying other documents. This is an appeal from the Military Hospital, from the staff of the Military Hospital, and it was taken over by others from the Srna News Agency. It is totally unacceptable to disqualify a news agency in this way, as far as news are concerned, not comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that we do not need to set up a new rule depending upon the content of the document. But simple or consistent application of our guide-line is that the witness didn't confirm anything about this, he gave his testimony about the content of this event, so we will not admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, now I'd like us to have a look at something. Actually, I'd like us to discuss medical documents, the medical documents that you provided. Is this everything that this hospital did, and, if so, in which period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which documents you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I mean the documents that are attached as medical documentation from this hospital that is often called the General Hospital of Sarajevo, and then the Military Hospital, and then the City Hospital. Is the General Hospital of Sarajevo the same thing as the Military Hospital or, rather, the State Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The State Hospital is the former Military Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what is this General Hospital of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a new term. That's a new term. Presently, that is the name it bears, the Hospital of Dr. Abdulah Nakas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did it become the General Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been about five or six years now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 09595, but I believe that it has a P number now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just while we're waiting for the exhibit number to come up: Mr. Karadzic put to the witness "medical documents that you provided." It's clear from the witness's statement that he didn't provide them. He was shown certain documents by the OTP, and he commented on certain documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document has been admitted as Exhibit P1235.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say here that it's the General Hospital of Sarajevo, and is the date the 9th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written there. But in 1993, it was the State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Five years ago, it became the General Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really say for sure. I am not sure about the actual dates, but in 1993 it was the State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, look, let's try to find our way somehow. It was the OTP, then, that showed this to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document. This is a document. It has a stamp, it's got everything, but -- ah, no, no, no, no, no. Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Karadzic, this is what this game is about: This is a copy of the findings of 1993. It was copied out. Often, for the purposes of various commissions, excerpts were requested from medical documentation, and it says up here "Copy." That is to say, this was copied from the original findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. And where are the original findings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the patient had the original findings, he wouldn't have asked for this. He probably needs to exercise some rights in connection with this. Obviously, the patient had been wounded, and he's probably asking for some kind of rights, exercised on the basis of a disability or whatever. So he simply wanted the original findings to be copied many years later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, by your leave, I really have to be a lot more careful with these associated documents. Dr. Mandilovic never saw this document before, and we admitted it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Karadzic, the document is perfectly valid. However, you tried to confuse me with the name of the hospital. It is absolutely valid, the document. You speak our language, don't you? And it says up here "Prepis Naliza" [phoen], that is to say, "Findings copied out for" such and such a person, and so on. And there's the date as well. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, Doctor. But why did we not receive a photocopy of the original findings? Why did we just get this copy that was written out a couple of days ago?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could not, because the lady obviously lost the original findings somewhere during the course of the war, and that is why she was asking for the original document -- for the original findings to be copied out. However, since we have excellent documents, we found her name, we found her diagnosis, and we simply wrote this out and said that she was wounded, and what the diagnosis was, and so on and so forth. It's hard for me to say now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I think that such documents should not be admitted through this witness; rather, these documents should be admitted through the person who actually copied them out, who wrote them out. Are these findings going to remain in evidence or will you have them withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, Dr. Mandilovic confirmed the way and as to how it is issued by the hospital, and he confirmed the authenticity. There's no reason not to admit this. And he confirmed in his statement that the -- in para 117 and 118, he confirmed the authenticity of these documents. On that basis, we admitted this document, and there's no reason for us to revisit the issue. Please carry on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have another page of this same document? If Dr. Mandilovic is familiar with this document, then let's have a look at it. The next page -- or, rather, 2, 3 -- page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, why was that needed? Because over here, you can see on the first page the actual patient history. So why was that copy needed when there is a patient history, without a stamp, in all fairness, but something is written here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document that I have on my screen now is perfectly valid, just like those findings. Now, why did the lady need the document, why did she need to have the findings copied out, I don't know. But both documents are absolutely valid.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 7, could we have that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, this is somebody else, some person called Meliha in this document, then Admir.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just have the case history signed by Dr. Ranko Vuletic. I don't have the first page, so I don't know the name and surname of the patient. I see that it's a valid document because it was signed by a doctor who I know personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this child was injured by whose bullet? Who was it that wounded this child?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say in the case history. It just says what the date was, that the child was brought to the ward after having been injured by a projectile and was immediately re-animated, and then the actual surgery performed is explained in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 65 ter 09615 now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, this has been admitted as Exhibit P1237.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is this wound; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an explosive wound in the right foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the person was released after two days; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say here: "Discharged on the 7th of February, 1994," Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It is barely legible, the original that I see here. I just see the name and surname. I see it says "civilian," and I see that this person was born in 1973. I see the address, Humska Street, 27. I have the diagnosis, and I see what was done; that the wound was dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And underneath?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Discharged on the 7th of February, 1994."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So she was released on the 7th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Vulnus," as it is written here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Because there are several findings with the very same word.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, of course, we didn't have 100 doctors, Mr. Karadzic. Our doctors were there in surgery and at the Emergency Ward. It's one and the same doctor who wrote up all these documents, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Vulnus," is that the same handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it's got to be the same doctor, no dilemma about that, the very same handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. And this person was released two days later as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the way we had to operate. We didn't have enough room. We would treat patients, and when there was no danger of further complications, we discharged patients, and then they were asked to come back for check-ups. This is an explosive wound of the right arm; that is to say, that the patient is perfectly mobile and we were in no position to keep that patient in hospital any longer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is also the 5th of February, Sefik Kukavica, civilian?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did the doctor come to this information, that this person was a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's very simple. Mr. Sefik came to the Surgery Ward on the 5th of February, and he showed documents showing who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's the same handwriting; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Karadzic, you worked in medical institutions. For heaven's sake, you can see it's the same date, and you can see that it is one single doctor who was working throughout that day at the Surgery Ward. It's different patients, but of course it's the same handwriting. It's the same day in surgery. Of course, it's the same man; of course, it's the same handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And they all waited for him to see them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who else could see them? I apologise. These are not urgent cases. These are people who come for a check-up and to have their wounds dressed. These are not people whose lives are in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, this is the 5th of February, so this is an exit/entry wound, we see, in the abdomen; explosive, hemi-thorax, all right, limbs, arm, leg. But look at all of this. They are all waiting in the waiting room to be received by that doctor. He's receiving them one by one, and he's dealing with them. It says "PHO." Can we have the next -- no, no, no, this is it. The next one, actually. That's it. Now the next one. Next one, please. "Vulnus sclopetarium"; right? What is this? "Slatizan [phoen] history." "Surgical treatment of wound." Can we have the next one? This is an exit/entry wound, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, of the gluteal area, right area. An anti-tetanus serum was administered, and the individual was hospitalised. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the person was discharged on the 8th of February; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So these are all patients following the explosion at Markale, and a doctor would line them up, take them in one by one, discharge them, or hospitalise them. So how does this all seem to you, as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very well. You have to know that serious cases were being operated in surgeries at this very moment and that there was a doctor there to receive less-serious patients. We used to have a triage conducted, prioritising patients for treatment. So if we are talking about this period, you are, in fact, bringing confusion into this whole matter. We have serious cases being treated in the theatre; whereas, less-serious cases were being treated in this ward. Most of the surgeons were being engaged in operations at this very moment, whereas there was just one surgeon, with the assistance of a nurse, who treated these less-serious cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, have you reviewed all the material shown to you by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was very voluminous. I don't know if I've seen everything, but I've seen a large part of it, and I stand by what I say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at 09616, a 65 ter document which probably has a P number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has been admitted as Exhibit P1238.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need to have the document in English. Could we have the entire document up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who added this in handwriting, "Shell"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the third column.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me a name? I don't see a "shell" written anywhere. Ah, now I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's evidently a different handwriting and a different pen. Who made these additional annotations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This is a different institution. It's a document from the Clinical Centre, and obviously somebody else made these additional annotations. However, from the description of the wounds, one can see that these were most probably -- this was most probably shrapnel, because we have "explosive wound," "explosive wound," "explosive wound." In other words, we had explosive wounds which were typical for shells.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Karadzic please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Dr. Mandilovic. Could you repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic. The interpreters couldn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the letter K stand for "Kuca," meaning "in-house" or "house"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible. This is the Clinical Centre after all, but it is possible. We have reception or hospitalisation with the first and the second cases as well; whereas, next to the case of Mira Stanisic, we have "K" there, so maybe meaning that she was actually discharged, sent home. Of course, there were less-serious wounds. Not all these cases were necessarily hospitalised.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to the next page. Another one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, it says two were discharged home?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the other two died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. How was it possible that a shell caused a vulnus sclopetarium, an entry/exit wound? We saw it in the Military Hospital. We have it here. How can we have an entry/exit wound as a result of a shell impact?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall there being such wounds. They were, for the most part, explosive wounds. And down here, if you look at the second patient from the top, we have combustion or, in other words, it's a burn. In the document we looked at earlier on, there was a sclopetarium wound, but it's really difficult to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it wasn't just one case. I'll find many more, as many as you like.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was constant fire, not just shelling. There was small-arms fire, there was sniper fire. It's difficult to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Hodzic -- no, 974 or page 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you identify the patient in the English page in which the exit and -- entry and exit wounds appear?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There, Patient 870, for instance. We have it here in the Serbian version, and it says clearly "Vulnus sclopetarium," "Regionis vateris femori sinistri." It says "sclopetarium," and it is added in handwriting "shell."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's possible. Why not? What does "sclopetarium" stand for? It means that it's an entry/exit wound. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Doctor, entry/exit wound?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. The shrapnel got in and got out and did not make extensive damage. It is quite possible. It need not always be an explosive wound. It can be a sclopetarium wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And need there be laceration, Doctor? How can shrapnel pass through tissue without lacerating it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shrapnel can be of different sizes. There are shrapnel -- there is shrapnel that can be smaller than a bullet, and, of course, they can get fragmented into thousands of pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 879, the next page, again we have the entry/exit wound?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 885, "Vulnus sclopetarium"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "Entry/exit wound." And that's as clear as day. I don't see why you should highlight it so. These are entry/exit wounds from shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 879, again "Vulnus trans-sclopetarium"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these were probably lucky people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the ones -- the individuals you're referring to were evidently lucky.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To be hit by a bullet; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, to have had the projectile go in and out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Come on, Doctor. You, yourself, don't believe what you're saying. How is it possible that you would have so many cases of vulnus sclopetarium as a result of a shell? Be a doctor and tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said what I've experienced, myself, and I stand by what I said. But I cannot stand behind every diagnosis made and every doctor's findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 5, can we look at Person number 863. "Vulnus sclopetarium." 861, "Vulnus sclopetarium."

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, fine. This was minor damage. Shrapnel got in and went out. The diagnosis is quite clear. I don't see why you're belabouring the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 858, 859, 860, it only says "Shell"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's move along. Let's look at page 1. "Vulnus sclopetarium, regionis vateris femori sinistri." We will not be mentioning the name. It says "Page 1." I'm not looking at the collective findings, but individual findings, so it's one page ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A page before the one we're seeing right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Karadzic doesn't want the witness's name to be spoken, perhaps we can go into private session or the document can be taken off the broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether this has already been broadcast, but --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any particular wish to mention the names. We simply don't need them. Perhaps we need not broadcast beyond the courtroom what we have on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At page 42, again we have the Military Hospital, again "Vulnus sclopetarium."

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you don't want us to mention names --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. But it was not tendered confidentially. It was admitted publicly. Just out of --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no problem, Your Honour. I wonder why Dr. Karadzic said that, and I thought there might be a reason for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It just -- I think it was out of an abundance of caution, but it is a public document. But let's carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. No problem. Can we go back, then, to the very beginning of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can only read out numbers. We don't need to mention first and last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. These numbers, 09 -- yes, these numbers, we can read them out. 65 ter 09959 -- 09595. It's been admitted already. It says "Vulnus sclopetarium, abdominis, hospitalisation."

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The diagnosis is more than clear, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first one we looked at.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Vulnus trans sclopetarium abdominis" is very clear. It means that the shrapnel entered the abdomen and left the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. This is not important anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are some documents here from the Military Hospital. I wonder, Your Excellencies, if the Defence should have allowed for documents originating from other hospitals to be admitted through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If documents originating from his hospital were admitted through this witness, I wonder perhaps -- should we have also introduced documents looking from some other hospital? I don't know which hospital this comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says "Military Post," doctor, does it not, up here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? Can you direct me to the spot you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the longest column, "Findings," "Opinions" -- no, and now it says, the first column. It says: "Names," "Military post," and "place." Describe -- or, rather, write the personal identification number -- can you see that, above the names, themselves? It says "Military Post" there, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "Military Post, "Place," and "Address," and, of course, all the other details concerning patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who does this document belong to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a medical document. It's a universal medical document. It doesn't say who it belongs to, but it's standard. This is something that we referred to during the earlier sessions, that we needed to have the patient's particulars; name, last name, address. We had to know whether the person was a civilian, what his occupation was, if he was a serviceman, what the details were, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And which hospital is this, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's the State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's the document there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see the protocol is the same. If you don't have a signature, if you don't have a stamp, you won't know who it belongs to, because the templates -- the forms are always the same. But I believe that this belonged to the State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we, based on the wounds described herein, draw conclusions as to who inflicted them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot. A wound is a wound. We can approximately tell whether the wound was the result of a shell shrapnel or anything else, but we can't establish that. This would be beyond my powers and beyond my role.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A general question, Doctor: How many post-mortems can a doctor carry out during the course of a single day? Forensic or pathology, they are very similar, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are very similar; I agree. It depends on the doctor, it depends on his knowledge, on his skill, on his motives. It's very hard to say. He can carry out post-mortems all night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if he works all day, how many can he carry out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say, 10 to 15, no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't know how much time I have left, Your Excellencies, so I'm cutting things short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm advised that you will have about an additional 15 minutes, but I'm of the impression that you can conclude in 5 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I have to deal with fewer documents. 1D2120.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, did you know Vesna Pagon?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have that document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2120. I don't know whether we have a translation, but it bears an OTP number -- an ERN number, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, can you have a look at this. Do you agree that this is Vesna Pagon, and it says that she has a Master's Degree in Pharmacology and that she worked in the pharmacy of the former Military Hospital of Sarajevo? Do you agree that that's what it says in the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here, but I don't know the lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's see what this lady doctor says. I shall interpret it, and you check on what I'm saying. So this is an interview at the State Security Service, at the Department of Novo Sarajevo. The date is the 8th of October, 1994. This lady says that she crossed over to the Serb territory through Kabil Amra, through the Commission for the Exchange of Civilians, and she was -- that person was Deputy of Amor Masovic. And then she says that the situation in the Military Hospital culminated because there are too few people working there, and doctors who are not professional enough are in different positions in the hospital. She gave, as a good example, Dr. Nakas, Abdulah, who protects Serb personnel who still work there. He is an eminent doctor, but he doesn't have support because he's not a member of the SDA. She says that Nakas is still in touch with doctors of Serb ethnicity, his former colleagues, who are now in Serb territory. As for his brother, Nakas, Bakir, she says that as opposed to Abdulah, he's turned into a major fundamentalist, on account of which he clashes frequently with his brother. As for ethnic Serbs who still work at the hospital, Vesna says that there are only about 30 of them left and they all want to leave Sarajevo and to cross over into Serb territory. Ethnic Muslim doctors are trying to prevent that in every conceivable way, and if somebody leaves all of a sudden, they say that it will not be a good thing, it causes panic in the hospital. They say it's not good if all the Serbs leave, because they are quite professional and they do their job professionally. Do you know who it was that left?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly now, but perhaps I can give a comment in respect of what you quoted just now. This is what I can say: I express my great dissatisfaction in relation to this document. I don't know what to call it. It absolutely does not correspond to the truth. Dr. Abdulah Nakas was a doctor, first and foremost, who helped everyone, irrespectively. Dr. Bakir Nakas was the manager of the hospital throughout and, as I said earlier on, he has enormous merit, in terms of keeping the hospital going. I did not notice anything extremely nationalist about any of these doctors. However, in respect of this pharmacist, I have to say the following: The first three surgeons at the State Hospital, after they left the JNA - one was a Montenegrin, another one was a Serb, and one was a Muslim, too - the chief of the group of Internal Medicine in our hospital was a Slovak, so this was really a multi-ethnic group of people and multi-religious as well. This was our main characteristic that we preserved throughout the war. That is why I think that we survived as such, and we were always guided by the idea of anti-fascism. As for these qualifications that I read here, I categorically renounce them and they do not correspond to the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you were guided by the idea of anti-fascism, are you talking about the Second World War or this war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This war, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was a fascist, Doctor? Who was it that you fought against?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We fought against aggression, against a terrible aggression that went on for 44 months incessantly, without interruption. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who carried out an aggression against who?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're shelling an area all the time, and if people cannot leave that territory, it is well known who it is that is carrying out this aggression. You don't have to be terribly clever to realise who it is. After all, you can ask all the many foreign observers who were there; professional monitors in UNPROFOR, then the European monitors. Then you should ask the media who were present in Sarajevo. I think they know that full well, and I think that they presented it very well, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, would you accept the formulation of the Security Council of the United Nations with regard to this particular topic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to give me an actual quotation so that I would know whether to accept that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there anyone competent there? You spoke of international factors. Is there anyone who has greater competence than the Security Council of the UN, and the Security Council said that this was a tragic conflict, not an aggression?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as an individual, cannot accept that as a conflict, because a conflict has -- goes on over a definite period of time, not over 44 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Conflicts can go on for 30 years and 100 years. There are wars that went on for a hundred years.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, wars, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know how long the Court wants to encourage this particular debate to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It ended, I think. Are you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, debate. The doctor says something that cannot remain unchallenged. He says something that is new. He gives his opinion as if he were an expert here, and I have to put it to him that the United Nations, that he referred to, termed the conflict in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, all right, Doctor. Do you know how many doctors from Sarajevo left Sarajevo, as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that exact figure, but a considerable number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned at one point that you had heard that Professor Najdanovic got killed. Was he your professor too?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Professor Najdanovic was stabbed, beaten up, and thrown into a garbage container?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never heard of that before I heard it from you just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever mention that he was a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was, yes. He was quite active in 1991, when the multi-party system was developing in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think he was one of the SDS leaders, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was a federal MP in the Federal Parliament of Yugoslavia and also a republican MP in the Joint Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about the federal level, but I think he was an MP at republican level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say, I heard that he got killed, but he was a member of the SDS, is that a sufficient reason for an eminent professor, a great doctor, a wonderful man, married to a Jewish lady, now that we're on the subject, is that reason enough for him to be killed and to be thrown into a garbage dump, a container?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will hear from you first, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that wasn't what the witness said. And if Mr. Karadzic is going to put something the witness said to him, he needs to -- he needs to say exactly what the witness said. In the supplementary information sheet that was provided to Mr. Karadzic, of the 14th of July, 2010, the witness -- it states that: he stated -- when asked about Professor Dr. Najdanovic, Dr. Mirko Sosic, and Marko Vukovic, he stated that they all worked at the Sarajevo University Clinical Centre and were members of the SDS. The witness stated that he heard that Professor Dr. Najdanovic died but did not know the circumstances of his death. He didn't say what Mr. Karadzic just put to him, that he died and he was a member of the SDS and so that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, how much longer do you have? Conclude in three minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three minutes, I'll conclude in three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, Doctor. Why did you find it necessary to say that they were members of the SDS in relation to their flight from Sarajevo and in relation to the death of Dr. Najdanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that has nothing to do with their flight from Sarajevo. I referred to 1991 and the period of extensive activity of the political parties that were being established after the disintegration of Yugoslavia. One of these parties was the SDS, that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How was it that you found out that Sosic and Vukovic were members of the SDS when they were never members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that they were members of the SDS. As a matter of fact, I said that I thought that Najdanovic was a member of the SDS. Sosic and Vukovic worked at the centre and perhaps they were members of the SDS, perhaps they weren't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you admit this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in the meantime, Doctor, with the permission of the Trial Chamber, I'm going to remind you of an anecdote, as they say: That all Jews and all cyclists are going to be arrested, and people say, why cyclists? See, so nobody asks, why Jews. So you're doing the same thing with the SDS, since you said members -- that they were members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing to do with the SDS. I have nothing to do with Professor Najdanovic. I really cannot give you proper answers to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: According to our consistent guide-line, we'll not admit this previous statement of Vesna Pagon, which the witness did not confirm any content of the document. It's a third party's document. We'll not admit that. Yes, Ms. Sutherland, did you have something else?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I was just going to say that Dr. Karadzic should refrain from making those sorts of comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you are concluded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any redirect examination, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Five minutes, but I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether we can continue. We started almost at 20 to. I think we can go on about five minutes. If you're confident in concluding in five minutes, I think we can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, Mr. Karadzic put to you, on page 69, starting at line 24 -- he asked you, had you reviewed all of the material shown to you by the Prosecution. And your answer was: "Well, it was very voluminous. I don't know if I've seen everything but I've seen a large part of it, and I stand by what I said." Just to be clear, if we can go to your amalgamated witness statement, which is Exhibit P1217. First of all, were you talking about the documentation, as a whole, the medical records the Prosecution holds or, in particular, the documents that you were particularly shown by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you very briefly. All the medical documents that you showed me and that the OTP presented to me, I confirmed them and I stand by them. As for the document that appeared here, I'm not sure it was from the OTP or from the Defence. That's why there was a bit of a dilemma. But I did not challenge or contest the validity of the documents at any point. All of the documents were perfectly valid, perfectly proper, with stamps, with the names of physicians, and diagnoses. That is why there was a bit of insecurity on my part. If all of these documents come from the OTP, I reviewed all of them and I stand by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Mandilovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. At the beginning of today's session, I took Your Honour to -- I mentioned that Mr. Karadzic had referred to a previous witness's testimony, and I just wanted to take to you that page. And that was page 5351, and it started at line 5. And may I be excused, Your Honour, because we need to make way for Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, who is taking the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Taking advantage of about two or three minutes, I I'm minded to give a ruling in relation to the motion filed by Mr. Karadzic on 16 July 2010 to exclude evidence of unscheduled shelling incidents from the testimony of Ekrem Suljevic, who is due to testify later this week. The Chamber has considered the submissions made in that motion, as well as in the Prosecution's response thereto filed on 19th July 2010, to determine whether it should exclude parts of Mr. Suljevic's testimony that go to shelling incidents in Sarajevo in the period relevant to the indictment, but which are not specifically listed in Schedule G to the indictment. The accused has noted that the Chamber's decision on the fifth Prosecution motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts, which declined judicial notice of a number of facts relating to such unscheduled incidents and argues that a similar approach should be taken to the evidence of Mr. Suljevic. However, decisions on the relevance of certain evidence to these proceedings are made on the basis of considerations that are not coterminous with those that apply when deciding to take judicial notice of adjudicated facts. Moreover, as noted by the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber has previously permitted evidence to be led concerning incidents and events in Sarajevo which are not listed in one of these schedules to the indictment, on the basis that such evidence may go to establishing the necessary general requirements for crimes against humanity or to the elements of some of the underlying offences. The Chamber emphasised that detailed evidence going to specific incidents which are not listed in the indictment or its schedules is unhelpful, as the Chamber would not ultimately be making beyond reasonable doubt findings as to the responsibility of the accused for such specific incidents. Having reviewed the proposed Rule 92 ter statements of Ekrem Suljevic in this light, the Chamber does not consider it necessary or appropriate to exclude parts thereof at this stage. However, it advises the Prosecution to be rigorous in its selection of those exhibits to tender through Mr. Suljevic and to avoid those that provide great amounts of detail about incidents which are not listed in Schedule G of the indictment. With this warning, the Chamber hereby denies the accused's motion to exclude evidence of unscheduled shelling incidents. We'll now rise and we'll have a break for 25 minutes. We'll resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon again to all. Welcome to the Tribunal, General Abdel-Razek. If you could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May God be my witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable, General. Welcome back, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. It's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Retired Major General Hussein Ali Abdel-Razek.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you provided statements to the Office of the Prosecutor and also testified here at the Tribunal in the Galic case in 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Today, we are only concerned with your statement of 16 July 2002 and the corrections that you made to that statement at that time. General, have you had opportunity to review this particular statement when you came to the Tribunal this time?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, I've had that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you say that the statement of 16 July 2002 accurately reflects the evidence you've provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, would you provide that same evidence to the Court if questioned on the same matters here today?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender the statement of 16 July 2002, as Exhibit 65 ter 08766 for admission under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1258, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I would now read a short summary of the witness's evidence, as admitted. General Abdel-Razek was commander of Sector Sarajevo of UNPROFOR from 21st August 1992 to 20 February 1993. During this time, he met with civilian leaders of the warring factions, including the accused, as well as military officials, including Stanislav Galic, the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and General Mladic. General Abdel-Razek regularly received reports from UN Military Observers about the constant shelling of the city by Serb forces and of sniping perpetrated against civilians. In addition, the witness himself made observations of random shelling and specific targeting of civilians. General Abdel-Razek and other UN officials frequently protested to Bosnian Serb officials the sniping and shelling attacks; in particular, attacks against the main hospital, the bus station, the market-place, and water lines. UNPROFOR also made written complaints to General Mladic and the accused.
