Generals Galic and Mladic, as well as Karadzic, Plavsic, Krajisnik, and Koljevic regularly denied that the Bosnian Serbs were responsible for the shelling or sniping. They claimed that the Bosnian government forces shelled their own people to gain support from the international community or that the VRS was only responding in self-defence. With respect to complaints about sniping against civilians at the airport, in particular, General Galic said that the VRS would continue this practice in order to stop all movements in that area. General Abdel-Razek observed a functioning chain of command within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, headed by General Galic, who reported to General Mladic. SRK troops and subordinates of military groups appeared to be professional, well-trained, and equipped. In a meeting requested by the accused after the London Conference, the accused spoke to the witness about future borders and said that Muslims were to be removed from Serb territories and Serbs from Muslim territories. On another occasion, the accused told General Abdel-Razek that the Serbs could not live together with the Muslims any longer. The accused referred to historical events and said that they would not allow this to happen again and that they may not again have such a chance. Krajisnik, Plavsic and Generals Mladic and Gvero were present on that occasion and shared Karadzic's views. The witness also attended a meeting with Krajisnik, Koljevic, and Plavsic, where Krajisnik expressed similar views on the issue of ethnic cleansing. In a meeting on 2nd October 1992 with Ms. Plavsic, General Abdel-Razek raised the issue of the expulsion of 300 Muslims from Grbavica and the removal and detention of three Muslim drivers from a UN convoy. Typical of Bosnian Serb leadership responses to such protests, Plavsic promised to look into these matters, but nothing ever resulted. Your Honour, this concludes the summary, and I will now ask some additional questions and also put some documents to the general.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you described your training and career in the Egyptian Army from 1964 onwards in your statement. Did your training and career include the use of artillery and combined arms and tactics?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. I have undergone all basic training in tactics, military tactics, and I am certified as battalion or regiment commander, and I have graduated from the Staff College and have obtained the highest level of qualification. I have participated in military manoeuvres within the Egyptian Army or in combined manoeuvres with other armed forces of other nations. For a while, I was in charge of the combined armed manoeuvres with foreign forces. I was involved in three wars with the Egyptian Army in Middle Eastern conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have experience in peacekeeping activities before coming to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. Before joining my post in Sarajevo, I was part of the Military Observation Force in Angola for a full year. Our role was to monitor the agreement between UNITA movement and the Angolan government before being asked by the Secretary-General of the UN to lead the United Nations forces in Sarajevo to replace General MacKenzie.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the UNPROFOR mission, can you tell the Court what your main sources of information were and whether they were reliable?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. I asked the -- asked the assistant secretary-general, Mr. Marrack Goulding, when he personally asked me moved to Sarajevo, I asked Mr. Goulding to provide me with some of the information that related to the situation in the former Yugoslavia, especially in the Sarajevo Sector, and he faxed me from New York, to Angola, several documents that outlined the most recent developments and the situation on the ground in Sarajevo. And he mentioned specifically to me the suspension of flights, especially relief flights, to Sarajevo -- into Sarajevo, but he assured me that these flights would be resumed, and asked me to join -- or to go to Zagreb first and to meet with General Nambiar, who was in command of the forces in Yugoslavia. I also had the opportunity to meet with the ambassador of Serbia to Angola, and I was able to obtain sufficient information to allow me to start my mission in the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And during your time in Sarajevo, what were your main sources of information?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: According to the procedures of work within the United Nations, there are military observers based in various sectors where the situation was conflictual, and those military observers operated under the supervision of a commander, and this commander of the observer force would communicate with me on the latest developments that occurred in the various sectors.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you described in your statement your meetings with the military commanders; in particular, General Galic. And you also mentioned that Ms. Plavsic took part in such meeting. Why did she attend, and what was her role during the meetings?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I'm personally not aware why she was present, that is, Ms. Plavsic. When I used to ask for meetings with General Galic, Ms. Plavsic attended these meetings. And when the meetings took place in several occasions, she used to lead the other side in the interventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From your observations during the meetings you had with the Bosnian Serb political and military leaders, and from the information you received, did the civilian and the military personnel pursue the same objectives?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that with certainty. And as I said, when Ms. Plavsic attended, she was leading the other side, an intervention, and she was the main speaker -- the main interlocutor on the other side. And we, the military personnel, only contributed every now and then to issues relating to the military situation, but she led all the interventions from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would ask that Exhibit 10670 be brought up on the screen, please. And as it is coming up: It is a fax from Mr. Goulding to the UNPROFOR Commander Nambiar, in Zagreb, of 28 August 1992, regarding the London Conference and the agreement achieved. We have here the cover letter. And the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, did you have the opportunity to study this document when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: No, I did not have the opportunity to see this document before my arrival, but I was made aware of its presence by General Nambiar when he received me upon assuming my responsibility. He met with all the sector chiefs, including myself, and he informed me that during the London Conference there was agreement reached with the Serbian side, and the Serbian side had expressed the desire to reach a -- conclude an agreement with the United Nations, and that the United Nations take responsibility of the collection of heavy weapons. But I have not seen that document before my arrival in The Hague this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were you aware of what Dr. Karadzic and Dr. Koljevic had agreed upon, as it is stated here in that main paragraph in the document, that is, heavy weapons to be grouped around the four towns, weaponry grouped -- the Bosnian Serb would expect the Bosnian government to take reciprocal action, and so on and so forth? Were you made aware of this?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: In fact, I felt there was optimism within the UN -- within UN circles when Dr. Karadzic declared, following the -- or in the wake of the London Conference, that these heavy weapons would be handed over, and I believe that was on the 11th of the month. And there was indications that we need to get ourselves into a state of readiness to oversee -- to observe the hand-over of these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request the admission of this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1259.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would ask that Exhibit 65 ter 10622, page 1, be brought up onto the screen, please, in both languages. And as it is coming up: It is a letter from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps Command of 30 August, 1992, to all units of the corps, providing a report about the London Conference on 26 and 27 of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, in your talks with the Prosecution personnel the last two days, did you have an opportunity to read this document?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It says here, on the first page -- it says here, in the second paragraph: "... you are obliged to acquaint all members of the units under your command with its content, and especially to pay close attention to the consistent implementation of the recommended measures in the units and commands at the end of the report." General, given your experience as a military commander, are troops pre-briefed in the way described here in this document about agreements made by political bodies? Is that a regular procedure or not?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: In some countries, there is such a policy where military instructions have this political element incorporated into it to make commanders aware of what led to that decision. I would say that there is a possibility such instructions are given, that is to say, political instructions to military commanders, if the situation is very complex or very precarious.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we have the last page, please, in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you see here that Assistant Commander General Gvero is signing this report. Did you meet this commander in your talks?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I would only meet with General Gvero in the presence of General Mladic in the course of the meetings of the joint military committee, whereby senior military commanders from the three sides would meet in the airport under the facilitation or the co-ordination of General Morillon. So that's the only time where I met General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in paragraph 8 on that same page, a bit higher up, it says: "Ensure that all measures which the Serbian republic's delegation pledged to carry out or that arise from the conference documents are consistently implemented." General, did you see this order being implemented on the ground?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: In fact, no, and that's why I raised this issue with Mr. Karadzic. And he explained to me, when I met him in Pale, that that was not the case, but he made it clear to me that was not what he intended to say or what he said was misinterpreted, and that the United Nations would only oversee the process, and that the UN would not be involved in handling weapons physically. He said that 11 points -- collection points were designated, and that designation of the 11 points would allow the UN to see what's happened in these 11 points. In fact, this did not materialise, and a lot of the issues that we were hoping or would like to have happen did not take -- did not materialise.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P1260.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we now have Exhibit 65 ter 10671 be brought up. And as it is coming up: It is a code cable of General Nambiar to Mr. Goulding of 14 September 1992, and a report attached regarding a meeting with Dr. Karadzic and Colonel Siber. Can we have the -- that's the cover letter. Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, is this a report that you made?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that this report existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is the report a correct reflection of the meeting that you had with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: The meeting was shrouded in optimism, to start with, and I felt that we were going to proceed with the collection of weapons. However, I noticed that the Serbian side was determined to retain these weapons, and I remember that they mentioned a reason for that. They said that the Muslim side outnumbered them, and that's why they needed to have the heavy weapons to counter-balance that numerical superiority. And I remember Mr. Karadzic was full of optimism, himself, and he was talking about steps of showing hope of improving the situation. He was talking about providing oxygen cylinders for the hospital. So that's what we were all hoping to achieve after the process.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Under B, it refers to Dr. Karadzic's opinion not to have the Egyptian troops involved in the monitoring. Why was that? Did he give you an explanation why?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: This opinion was not expressed to me directly or openly, but I believe he expressed that opinion to General Nambiar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And why was that? Do you know why he had some reservations?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: My understanding from him at a later stage, that had to do with the security situation. He gave the impression that his own people in certain instances would not accept Egyptian troops because of their faith, because of their leanings, and he thought that they would be -- they would not be safe being present on Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would now -- Your Honour, I request the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit P1261.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would now like to ask Exhibit P1004 be brought up, the first page in both languages. And as this is being brought up: It is an order from the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, dated 5th September 1992, related to the preparation for a meeting with the political leadership on 6 September.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, did you have an opportunity to review this document when you came here in the last two days?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The second page, please, in the English. The B/C/S is correct as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It refers here to where the meeting is supposed to take place. It says here "Rajska Valley, Jahorina Mountain." Do you know what place that is --

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, and we did meet once before in this position with Ms. Plavsic and the Serbian delegation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document was admitted in the decision on Prosecution submission on the relevancy of certain documents relating to the testimony of Richard Philipps, dated 9 July 2010, a source document. I request the admission of this exhibit into evidence now for all purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your notice. It well-noted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And it will be admitted as you indicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would ask that Exhibit P2006 be brought up onto the screen, and the first page in both languages, please. 1006. Did I say something differently? I'm sorry, 1006. I misspoke. And as this is being brought up: It is a document from the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, dated 12 September 1992, to the corps's rear command post, and it relates to the 6 September meeting and task list.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, did you also review this document while -- during the last two days here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 - that's at the bottom in both languages - it says: "Ensure absolute agreement and unity with the civilian authorities and MUP forces at all levels. Eliminate the creation of any paramilitary units or para-political groups, and eliminate any squabbles because we have the same goal." General, did you observe such co-operation as is requested here on the ground?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. There were serious attempts that I noted within the Romanija Corps, and they were trying to put control on the paramilitary forces in the region because some of these forces were creating many problems, because they did not enjoy the same level of discipline that military -- regular military forces demonstrate. Some of them acted in light of their own emotions. And, of course, such instructions should be given in order to provide for unity and for lack of discipline or disobedience against orders issued by the commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we have the next page, please, in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in paragraph 9, it says here: "Study all the requests made by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps commander and the civilian authorities, and do everything possible to act on them ..." General, as a military officer with experience in combat, do you have any comment on the fact that the rear command post is requested to respond to requests of the civilian authorities? Is there something -- is that special?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: According to my experience, I can say this was a civil war that took place in residential areas, and I expect that such instructions can be given to military commanders to co-operate more closely with civilian authorities in order to impose control and discipline on different parts of the country. And I can accept that such instructions be given in such a manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And further on --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The next page, please, the next page, in the English as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And here, if we look at paragraph 16, it says here -- it refers here to the Ministry of Interior and the Intelligence/Security Administration, and that they should make a plan. General, do you -- did you see co-operation between the military forces and the police on the ground?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I cannot say this with certainty because I was not directly involved in the field. However, in some locations I saw a degree of co-operation. And if we take Ilidza, we found, in certain command posts, many military and civilian personnel using the same rationale and acting in accordance with the guide-lines of the leadership. But in other places, we found matters to be completely different and each party did as it willed. Therefore, I cannot say this was specifically the case, because I was not everywhere. I can only speak of those locations that I visited. And I based my impression on what I saw. In some cases, they were in compliance with what we call discipline, and in other places, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in paragraph 18, it refers here to the behaviour towards the UNPROFOR and journalists. Was that reflected on the ground, this polite and correct behaviour towards UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: In fact, from the Serbian side and from the other parties, we were met with respect and warm hospitality and good arrangements for our meetings. But as I said earlier, the problem was always in the field, when we went to the field. Many of what -- of the arrangements we put in place and what we agreed on were not strictly adhered to in the field. On the contrary, we found that there was a degree of non-discipline by certain soldiers, certain individuals in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is another of the Philipps documents, and I would now like to tender it for all purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would now ask for Exhibit 65 ter 09083 be brought up on the screen. And as it is coming up: It is an order of Commander Galic to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, dated 16 November 1992, to all units.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in the first paragraph, it refers to a call from Professor Koljevic, requesting assistance from the SRK in manpower for the Herzegovina Corps for Nevesinje. And then following under "Order," we see that the Ilidza Brigade and other units are requested to make fighters available. Did General, did you see this document as well in the last two days?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as you have mentioned that you met Mr. Koljevic several times, to your knowledge, was he in a position to make requests to the Bosnian Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: In fact, I do not know what exactly is the competence of the senior or lower commanders in these forces, but I often discussed with them matters related to civilian affairs. Therefore, this document is very strange for me, to have a command to General Galic in this manner. I believe these matters are up to them, and these were not matters I was involved with. There may be a delegation from the senior command to Mr. Koljevic to present such orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admittance of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think this one goes outside of your guide-lines, in the sense that the witness really couldn't speak to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me then ask a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic, which role did he have, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Usually, Mr. Koljevic accompanied Mr. Karadzic, and I thought that he always addressed supreme political issues and was not involved in tactical matters and in military matters. And what I find strange in this document is that it is related to a military command, and I would ask: Where is General Mladic, who is the professional person of competence? For the Serbian corps, they should be getting their orders from General Mladic. Therefore, I did not know what exactly were the mandates given to them. This is some matter related to the Serbian side that I was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: An order given by a political leader in this way and responded to, would that be outside the regular chain of command?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I would say somebody has drafted this report in this military language. Perhaps Mr. Koljevic gave a general -- a broad guide-line, but then military leaders drafted it and he just signed his name. So I do not know how this reached Galic. Was it delivered to him by telephone or in the form of a letter, I do not know exactly. But I would imagine, from the text of these orders, this is a simple military order. It does not require a very high military professionalism. It is just a request for support from this sector to a certain quarter. It does not go into many technical details related to military issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I still request the admittance of this document as evidence. And it relates, in fact, to the evidence of this witness, who has stated here so far of the close co-operation between the military and the political leadership, and, therefore, I think it falls within the guide-lines of this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do maintain our objection, and, in principle, there's nothing objectionable about the document, itself. And with the proper witness or under other more relaxed guide-lines, the document could be admitted. But if this kind of standard that's being applied to the Defence documents, I think if it's going to be applied equally, this is not a witness who could speak to this. And, in general, civilian and -- any document -- military document which mentions contact with a civilian official is considered to be -- can be admitted under the same kind of argument that Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff has made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, did you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIGER
utterances.text: I was going to say that Mr. Robinson was not here for the entirety of the testimony of Mr. Mandic, during which a battery of documents were presented and admitted with -- well, military documents, in particular, by -- during the course of an examination of a witness who, at various times, purported to have very little information about the military chain of command. I raise that because contrary to Mr. Robinson's suggestion that there's some lack of equality here, documents have been coming in because of some form of contextualisation. I believe this witness has provided more than ample contextualisation in that context. And I believe if Mr. Robinson would take the opportunity to review the entirety of the documentation that was admitted during the course of that examination, he would see that there is no imbalance here, but that this document would properly come in under the same approach that was used previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is also important is the consistent application of the guide-line. While the witness testified to the close relation between the civilian authority and the military leaders, he was not aware of this incident, and then he cannot assist the Chamber in relation to this document. Certainly, this document can be a subject of further Bar table motion later on, but as I indicated, to apply the guide-line consistently we'll not admit this at this time. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say a word, by your leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I gave our ruling. In relation to this one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is in the translation. Had it said "appeal" instead of "call," the meaning would have been completely different as for this document. "Appeal," "appeal" is the word that should have been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you described throughout your statement meeting with Dr. Karadzic and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership. During such meetings, what role would Dr. Karadzic have?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic represented the head of the Bosnian Serbs or the head of the party, and he was at the top of the decisions related to the Bosnian Serbs. And, therefore, I always was concerned to meet with the relevant parties to be able to arrive with them at agreements that would facilitate the work of the United Nations, and, through them, to have the decisions reached that would affect those working in the field so that they will co-operate with us in the Sarajevo Sector. He represented the leader of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, General, you also mentioned meetings with both Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic in attendance. In such meetings when they were both together, what role would Dr. Karadzic have in such meetings?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: As I said, I would attend these meetings carrying with me a number of points to discuss with them in order to arrive at decisions related to the operations of the United Nations. In some cases, I would take with me certain claims that were reported to me, claims from the other parties, to raise in this meeting and to hear the response. And I would act the role of a mediator, I would play this role, although it wasn't one of my core competences, yet I did this voluntarily in order to help facilitate operations of the United Nations. I tried to build a degree of confidence with the parties in order to be successful in our work in the Sarajevo Sector. Therefore, he was always the spokesperson, and he had his assistants mentioned earlier by me. Some of them would sometimes give some comment, and this is normal. However, the head of a delegation usually consults with his assistants before responding to certain points. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you have opportunity to observe General Galic among his troops? And if so, how would they behave towards him?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I would notice him at his command centre. I would not go to the field. I would meet him at his headquarters in Lukavica. I know that there matters were run professionally towards command headquarters, and there were officers there who were co-operating with them, and I would describe relations as professional. However, I did not have the opportunity to see him among his soldiers, among the front-lines, or other such places in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to observe General Mladic with other generals and his subordinate commanders?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mladic would come to meetings of the joint military group, surrounded by his assistants, and I would note his strength and control. You can see him as a -- and as a military man, I can judge such matters. I felt him to be a strong man among his assistants.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, a few questions on the Sarajevo shelling. And I would ask that Exhibit 65 ter 10816 be brought up. And as it is coming up: We have here a note for Mr. Thornberry, dated 8 October 1992, related to the situation in Sarajevo. Do you know who made this note?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: If this is related to Mr. Thornberry, I believe the person concerned is the Civilian Affairs adviser in the sector command. It could be Mr. Adnan Abdel-Razek, perhaps, and there is always a confusion or misunderstanding between our names because we have the same family name. Mr. Adnan Abdel-Razek was an adviser for the sector commander for civilian affairs and within the liaison with Mr. Thornberry. He should send him the report, but he would present the report to me before sending it. Mr. Thornberry would collect his report from the different advisers on civilian affairs, and then it would go to Mr. Nambiar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It says here -- in paragraph 1, it says: "The general mood of Sarajevo people has reached the lowest level that I have seen since last April. The lack of water and electricity, together with the continuing shelling of civilian targets, have pushed people to their edge of tolerance and caused a high degree of despair and aggressiveness. People are lining up to leave the city." General, is that an accurate description of the situation of the people in Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Taking the date into account, I would say, yes, definitely; not only the population, but also the United Nations. Everyone was in despair, for the city was besieged and there was shelling and sniping and roadblocks and killing, and everybody was in this mood. And I found these feelings to be normal, in light of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't object to the admission of the document, but I think it ought to be clarified whether this witness is the author, because since he refers to "last April," and then this witness had only arrived in August, I think it's the other Abdel-Razek who was the author of the document, and that ought to be clarified; although, we don't have any objections since he confirmed part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he not clarify that issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, he said there was confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, he said there had been confusion among the two of them, but I didn't know that he was specifically directing that to this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The witness actually said that he thinks it was Adnan Abdel-Razek.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would now ask to show a very brief video-clip, and it is 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It is noted in page 108 from line 8. This will be admitted as P --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1262, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: A short video, 65 ter 45025 and is -- please be played, it's just a minute duration. And, General, I would like you to look at who you see in that video and whether you know where this is -- what is happening there. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But where's the voice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we supposed to hear something?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, we are supposed to hear Mr. Owen say something in English. Can it be louder?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or shall we try again?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I don't -- at least I heard him speak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that we don't have the transcript of this videotape.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The interpreter just said that they have the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, they don't. Sorry, I misheard. Okay, then we can't have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But what you saw here, do you recall what event it is, when you look at the people?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. I, myself, co-ordinated this meeting upon the headquarters in Zagreb, whereby Mr. Owen would be present to attend a meeting with Mr. Karadzic and his aides. I, myself, accompanied them to that meeting, as you can see from the tape. I remember well that was Mr. Owen, accompanied with General Morillon, and I was, myself, representing the United Nations. And from the other side, I remember Mr. Karadzic was there, General Mladic was also present, and Mr. Koljevic, if I remember well, was also present. This visit came as a result of the intensification of shelling and the complication and the exacerbation of the security situation, which culminated in the shelling on the hospital. Mr. Owen visited the hospital and spent some time there and talked to the doctors, and he was briefed by them on the problems faced at the hospital. And he carried from them a message to Mr. Karadzic, and that was the speech that we could not hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In that speech, did Owen address -- Lord Owen address the shelling and --

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: He mentioned that he visited the hospital and he was affected by the situation there, he was touched by the situation, but he was not there to express any opposition as to what happened. He was diplomatic in his words, but he wanted to say that something wrong happened in the situation there which culminated in the shelling of the hospital. We were all affected by the situation. I, myself, visited the hospital, and I saw for myself that the situation was so bad. Mr. Owen also raised a number of other topics, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we have to try a bit later, whether we can hear it, because I really want to tender it. But, of course, that's not possible right now. Can we please have Exhibit 65 ter 11350 brought up. And it is an UNPROFOR report from sector commander to the force commander in Zagreb, dated on 18 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is that your report about a flour mill damaged?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I think, yes, there was a lack -- penury of supplies, and I do remember that date very well. And I think there was an appeal for help from the Bosnian side, because they were facing a dire situation because of the penury in food supplies in the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So I request the admission of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be admitted as Exhibit P1263.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would now also try another video. I can only hope this time it works. It's 65 ter 45015.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, it's -- at least there is a transcript running. Can we start again?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to have played the section 00:09:52 to 00:11:25, and we would have to read what is actually here. Your Honours, I just hear we have to come back to this as well tomorrow because there is a wrong clip being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry. I would ask that Exhibit 65 ter 09922 be brought up. And as it is coming up: It is a very urgent order of Commander Galic to all RSK units of 10 October 1992, and -- well, that's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It should be 09122.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: 09122. Oh, yeah, I misspoke. Thank you. Yes, that's the correct one. It is a very, very urgent order, as it says on top, Commander Galic to all RSK units of 10 October 1992 to stop firing on the city of Sarajevo, as it says in the header. And it also states, in paragraph 2 -- there, it says that for using the heavy artillery, permission from the corps commander or his deputy is needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, did you have an opportunity to review this document within the last two days?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if you recall, what was happening on the 10th of October in Sarajevo that such an order would be given? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I think that was in the aftermath of the intensive bombing and shelling of Sarajevo, which led to a large number of casualties among the civilians. I did raise this question in many of the meetings I held with the other side. I think in October, that October, I noticed that there was intensive shelling at different areas in Sarajevo. I did raise this question. I think that was an order which was political in nature. I don't think that General Galic issued that order as a result of my protest against it, but I think he received orders from his higher commands. This could have been a result of a protest by Mr. Karadzic, thanks to the letters that I carried, that such an order was issued. As I see and you see, this order called for some kind of a cease-fire, and that in case of need, any forces can resort to the weapons at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In your statement, you referred also to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was admitted as Exhibit P1264.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In your statement, you also referred to Bosnian Serb sniper activities. And from the information you had and from your own observations, were these sniping activities random, or systematic, or both?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I did not really understand the question. What I understood is, from a professional standpoint, I think no -- not everyone who carries a gun is a sniper. I think the snipers are chosen among highly-qualified personnel and according to a plan devised by the command, the higher command. Not everyone who carries a gun can be considered a sniper. So the presence of snipers is decided upon a military plan that has been adopted and agreed upon by the military commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that Exhibit P1010 be brought up onto the screen, and it is another of Mr. Philipps' documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a source document?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, a source document. It is an order of the Deputy Commander Marcetic of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, of 4 November 1992, regarding designating locations for snipers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know this Colonel Marcetic? Can we see the signature a bit --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you go a bit further down? Oh, I think in -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's in the -- in the B/C/S version, you see "Dragan Marcetic." Do you know this colonel?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. He used to work with General Galic, and he used to attend some of the talks that we held there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to study this document within the last two days? And if so, what is it? For a military man, what is it?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Please give me some time to look at this document to know what it is. I have seen a number of documents on snipers. As you said, I think that goes along with what I said in the past. I think deploying snipers takes place in accordance with a plan devised by the higher command, and I think this document goes in the same sense that I have already explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would now like to have this document admitted for all purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the time, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer would you be?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, except for the two videos, I have to more documents or -- yeah, two more documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, General, we'll adjourn for today. We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of July, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
